# From continuous systems to discrete models {#sec-discrete-continuous}

In a discrete system, the state is described by a finite set of variables. In a
continuous system, the state is described by one or more fields defined over the
entire domain.

## A continuous system: a one-dimensional bar

![One-dimensional bar fixed at the left end, with
end force $F$, coordinate $x$, cross-sectional area $A$, Young's modulus $E$,
and axial displacement field
$u(x)$.](images/bar_in_tension-1d.png){
  #fig-bar-1d
  width=30%
}

A one-dimensional bar is a continuous body. Its axial displacement $u$ can be
evaluated at every point of the bar and is represented by a function,

$$
  u=u(x).
$$

The state of the bar is therefore described by the continuous displacement field
$u(x)$, which assigns a displacement value to every point along the bar.

The displacement field is the primary variable of the problem. Its variation
along the bar determines the axial strain. Under the small-strain assumption,
the axial strain is defined by

$$
  \varepsilon(x)=\frac{du}{dx}=u'(x).
$$

For a linearly elastic material, the axial stress is related to the strain by

$$
  \sigma(x)=E(x)\varepsilon(x).
$$

The corresponding axial resultant force is

$$
  N(x)=\int_A \sigma\,dA.
$$

Under the one-dimensional bar assumption that the axial stress is uniform over
the cross-section,

$$
  N(x)=A(x)\sigma(x).
$$

Using the linear elastic constitutive relation and the small-strain kinematic
relation,

$$
  \boxed{
  N(x)=E(x)A(x)\frac{du}{dx}.
  }
$$

![Cross-section $A$ with axial stress $\sigma_x$, represented equivalently by
the internal axial force $N$. A positive internal force corresponds to
tension.](images/bar-cross-section.png){
  #fig-bar-cross-section
  width=27%
}

## A discrete system: a one-dimensional spring

A spring is already a discrete mechanical system. Its state can be described by
quantities defined only at its end points.

![One-dimensional spring of stiffness $k_s$ between end points 1 and 2. The end
displacements $u_1$ and $u_2$ are referred to the positive
$x$ direction.](images/spring-1d.png){
  #fig-spring-1d
  width=27%
}

The spring elongation or spring stretch is a measure of the spring deformation
and is defined as

$$
  \delta=u_2-u_1.
$$

A positive elongation corresponds to a stretched spring. The internal spring
force is related to the elongation by

$$
  F_s=k_s\delta=k_s(u_2-u_1),
$$

where $k_s$ is the spring stiffness.

![Positive sign convention for the internal spring force $F_s$: outward forces
at the two sides of a cut spring indicate
tension.](images/spring-1d-convention.png){
  #fig-spring-1d-convention
  width=27%
}

## Continuous and discrete descriptions

The bar is described by the continuous displacement field $u(x)$, defined at
every point along its length, whereas the spring is described by the two
discrete displacement values $u_1$ and $u_2$. The continuous description is
therefore richer: it provides the displacement at every point, whereas the
discrete description contains only a finite number of displacement values.

This distinction is also reflected in the internal-force relations. For the
one-dimensional bar,

$$
  N(x)=E(x)A(x)\frac{du}{dx},
$$

so the internal axial force depends on the spatial variation of the continuous
displacement field. For the spring,

$$
  F_s=k_s(u_2-u_1),
$$

so the internal spring force depends on the difference between two discrete
displacement values.

The finite element method will later approximate a continuous field using a
finite set of unknowns. Before introducing that approximation, we begin with
springs, which are already discrete, and use them to develop the fundamental
algebraic ingredients of the method: equilibrium, element stiffness matrices,
assembly, boundary conditions, and the global system of equations.

These discrete ingredients provide the algebraic setting in which the direct
stiffness method can be developed.

::: {.callout-important title="Key points to remember"}
- A continuous model describes fields, such as $u(x)$, at every point of a
  domain; a discrete model has a finite set of state variables.
- For the one-dimensional bar, axial strain, stress, and internal force follow
  from $\varepsilon=du/dx$, $\sigma=E\varepsilon$, and $N=EA\,du/dx$.
- A spring is already discrete: its deformation and internal force depend on
  the end displacements through $\delta=u_2-u_1$ and $F_s=k_s\delta$.
- Finite elements approximate a continuous field with a finite set of unknowns;
  springs provide a direct route to the associated algebraic ideas.
:::
